content: 1. Nepal has revised its National Drinking Water Quality Standards to include specific water quality parameters and testing frequencies. These standards allow the use of approved portable water test kits with membrane filtration for microbial analysis, addressing challenges in consistent water quality data collection, especially for small supplies. By 2023, over 200 municipalities in Nepal were using these kits, contributing to the National Water Supply, Sanitation, and Hygiene Management Information System. 2. In Portugal, the Water and Waste Services Regulation Authority oversees drinking water quality and allows certified water operators to measure residual chlorine directly in the field. To ensure compliance and result comparability, a 12-page recommendation was developed in collaboration with accredited laboratories and other entities. This recommendation simplifies ISO standards for small water supply operators. 3. Bhutan’s National Guideline for Drinking Water Quality Surveillance (2019) and Drinking Water Quality Standard (2016) outline reporting requirements for surveillance data. Immediate reporting is required for non-compliant results threatening public health. The government is reforming the water supply sector, and updates to these guidelines are expected. 4. In the Philippines, the Code on Sanitation (1976) delegates drinking water quality surveillance to local government units, even for small supplies. Guidelines issued in 2022 clarify roles and responsibilities for surveillance and establish local monitoring committees. An operations manual provides detailed guidance on activities like water safety plan audits and sanitary inspections, with requirements for monthly, quarterly, and annual reporting. 5. In the United States, the Environmental Protection Agency mandates filtration and disinfection for public water supplies using surface water or groundwater influenced by surface water. Small water supplies are supported with guidance on technologies like chlorine disinfection, UV disinfection, and nanofiltration. These rules aim to reduce microbial contaminants in drinking water. 6. New Zealand’s 2022 Drinking Water Quality Assurance Rules require filtration, UV disinfection, and chlorination for supplies serving 101–500 people. Alternative compliance options, called acceptable solutions, provide ready-made regulatory pathways for specific water sources like roof water and springs. 7. Ghana introduced a standard in 2022 for household water treatment (HWT) products, defining performance classifications for pathogen removal and testing methods. A certification scheme was developed in 2023 to ensure compliance with this standard, providing clarity for manufacturers and importers regarding production practices and inspection schedules. 8. In Finland, the Health Protection Act requires water supply operators to undergo competency examinations every five years, covering water treatment technology, monitoring, legislation, and hygiene. These exams are mandatory for operators serving more than 50 people or providing over 10 m³ of water daily, with oversight by the National Supervisory Authority for Welfare and Health.
